title: Projected procedure volume growth
summary: The French expert forecasts a 15‑20 % annual increase in strong centres, the German expert expects high single‑digit to low double‑digit growth, and the UK clinician suggests possible growth above 15 % in some areas if training improves. All agree growth will occur, but the magnitude and certainty differ. The statements reflect different market expectations and hedging language.

positions.position: Adoption is expected to keep increasing steadily rather than explosively, with a possible 15 to 20 percent rise in procedures annually at stronger centres, while smaller hospitals stay slower.

evidence.quote: I expect adoption to continue increasing, probably steadily rather than explosively. I would expect maybe 15 to 20 percent more procedures annually in some of the stronger centres, but smaller hospitals will remain slower.

positions.scope: more procedures annually in some of the stronger centres

positions.position: Growth is likely to be in the high single digits or low double digits for procedure volumes, not as high as a 20 percent market-wide increase.

evidence.quote: I would expect continued growth, but probably closer to high single digits or low double digits in procedure volumes rather than something like 20 percent across the whole market.

positions.value: high single digits or low double digits

positions.position: The expert is quite positive about the next three to five years and could see procedure growth above 15 percent annually in some areas if training expands and systems become more cost‑competitive.

evidence.quote: I am quite positive. I think adoption could accelerate if training expands and systems become more cost competitive. I could see procedure growth above 15 percent annually in some areas.

title: Economic case drives decisions
summary: Finance and procurement leaders emphasise ROI, total cost of ownership and procedure volume as decisive factors. The UK clinician acknowledges ROI but also mentions patient outcomes and strategic positioning, adding a broader view. The positions are broadly aligned but differ in scope of considerations.

positions.position: Return on investment is crucial: finance teams need to see utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance costs and evidence that the system will ultimately pay for itself.

evidence.quote: Very important. The clinical argument may get surgeons interested, but the finance team wants to understand utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance cost and whether the system will actually pay for itself.

positions.position: Procurement decisions focus on total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts, and training, with the economic case ultimately determining approval.

evidence.quote: We look at total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts and training requirements. A strong clinical case helps, but the economic case decides whether it gets approved.

positions.position: ROI matters, but decisions are not purely financial; hospitals also consider patient outcomes, length of stay, surgeon recruitment, and whether the technology improves their clinical position.

evidence.quote: It matters, but the discussion is not always purely financial. Hospitals also consider patient outcomes, length of stay, surgeon recruitment and whether the technology improves their clinical position.

title: Procurement decision timeline
summary: The French urology head cites a six‑to‑twelve‑month window once a hospital is serious, the German director notes nine‑to‑eighteen months due to multiple stakeholders, and the UK consultant mentions six‑to‑nine months when funding is pre‑approved but longer otherwise. The ranges overlap but differ in typical duration and conditions. The perspectives vary by role and market context.

positions.position: A realistic purchase decision takes six to twelve months once a hospital is serious, though it can be longer if the capital committee pushes the purchase into the next budget cycle.

evidence.quote: Six to twelve months is realistic once the hospital becomes serious. It can be longer if the capital committee pushes the purchase into the next budget cycle.

positions.position: The procurement process typically takes nine to eighteen months, as multiple stakeholders must align.

evidence.quote: Nine to eighteen months is common.

positions.position: Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available; otherwise waiting for a new capital cycle can take much longer.

evidence.quote: Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available. If the trust has to wait for a new capital cycle, it can take much longer.

title: Training critical for utilization
summary: All three experts stress that having only one trained surgeon limits utilisation and weakens the business case. The French and German respondents highlight operational concerns, while the UK consultant adds that training capacity is as important as funding. Despite differing roles, the core message aligns.

positions.position: Training is especially important in the first year; if only one surgeon can operate the robot, the economics are difficult, so hospitals aim to have several surgeons trained to keep utilisation high.

evidence.quote: Training matters, especially in the first year. If only one surgeon can use the system, the economics become difficult. Hospitals want several surgeons trained so utilisation is high enough.

positions.position: Surgeon training is operationally critical; if only one surgeon is comfortable, utilisation will be poor, weakening the business case.

evidence.quote: Very important operationally. If the hospital buys a system but only one surgeon is comfortable using it, utilisation will be poor. That weakens the business case.

positions.position: Funding is important, but training capacity is just as important; without enough trained surgeons and theatre staff, adoption stalls even if a system is purchased.

evidence.quote: Funding is important, but I would say training capacity is just as important. You can buy a system, but if you cannot train enough surgeons and theatre staff, adoption stalls.

title: Uneven adoption across hospital sizes
summary: Clinicians and procurement experts observe that large academic or university hospitals adopt robotic surgery faster, whereas smaller regional hospitals adopt more slowly. This pattern is reported for France, Germany and the United Kingdom. The wording varies but the overall assessment is consistent.

positions.position: Adoption of robotic surgery is growing but remains focused in larger academic hospitals and private centres with strong capital budgets, while smaller regional hospitals adopt it much more slowly.

evidence.quote: Adoption is growing, but it is still concentrated in larger academic hospitals and private centres with stronger capital budgets. Smaller regional hospitals are much slower.

positions.position: Robotic surgery adoption is expanding overall but remains uneven, with large university hospitals being far ahead while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.

evidence.quote: It is growing, but adoption is quite uneven. Large university hospitals are much more advanced, while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.

positions.position: Adoption is increasing, with robotic surgery becoming standard in larger NHS trusts, but access still varies significantly by hospital.

evidence.quote: Adoption is increasing, and in some larger NHS trusts robotic surgery is becoming standard for selected procedures. But access still varies significantly by hospital.

title: Capital cost as primary adoption barrier
summary: Both the French urology head and the German procurement director identify the large capital outlay and budget approval process as the main obstacle to acquiring a robot. Their comments focus on the need for a strong economic case before purchase. The perspective is shared across different roles and markets.

positions.position: The biggest obstacle to adoption is capital budget approval; even if clinicians like the technology, purchasing committees require a strong economic case before authorising a purchase.

evidence.quote: The biggest issue is still capital budget approval. Hospitals may like the technology clinically, but purchasing committees need a strong economic case before approving a system.

positions.position: The primary barrier is cost, as these systems require large capital outlays and hospitals face financial pressure; a secondary barrier is demonstrating sufficient usage to justify the investment.

evidence.quote: Cost is the first barrier. These are large capital purchases, and hospital finances are under pressure.
The second issue is proving that the system will be used enough.

title: Clinical outcomes not decisive
summary: The French head of urology states that while good clinical outcomes are necessary, they are insufficient when two systems deliver similar results; economic factors then dominate the decision. This view is not echoed by the other experts, who focus on cost, training or broader strategic considerations. The comment reflects a clinician‑centric perspective on decision criteria.

positions.position: While good clinical outcomes are necessary, they are not enough; when two systems deliver similar outcomes, hospitals will focus on economics and utilisation to decide.

evidence.quote: Clinical outcomes are necessary, but they are not enough on their own. If two systems offer similar outcomes, the hospital will look hard at economics and utilisation.

title: Detailed procurement evaluation criteria
summary: The German procurement director outlines specific evaluation factors such as total cost of ownership, expected volume, maintenance, service contracts and training. None of the other experts provide a comparable checklist. The focus on granular procurement metrics reflects a procurement‑focused role.

positions.position: Procurement decisions focus on total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts, and training, with the economic case ultimately determining approval.

evidence.quote: We look at total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts and training requirements. A strong clinical case helps, but the economic case decides whether it gets approved.

title: Sustainability beyond purchase
summary: The UK consultant highlights that adoption requires not only the robot but also enough trained staff and sufficient procedure volume to sustain the programme. This emphasis on post‑purchase sustainability is not mentioned by the French or German respondents. The statement combines operational and strategic concerns from a clinical viewpoint.

positions.position: Adoption is not just about buying the machine; hospitals need enough trained people and sufficient procedure volume to make the programme sustainable.

evidence.quote: The key point is that adoption is not just about buying the machine. Hospitals need enough trained people and enough procedure volume to make the programme sustainable.
